objects: exact LMM association statistics; sample size n
assumptions: genome-wide association with many individuals and SNPs
conclusion: The cubic per-SNP cost of EMMA makes exact LMM testing impractical for moderately sized GWAS.
scope: Computational motivation for GEMMA; not a statistical failure of EMMA.
span: For example, at the time this work was submitted for publication, the most efficient algorithm for computing (effectively) exact association test statistics (either the Wald test or the likelihood ratio test), implemented in the Efficient Mixed Model Association (EMMA) software3, had a per-SNP computational time that increases with the cube of the number of individuals (n). As a result, a medium size GWAS with a few thousand individuals and half a million SNPs would take years of CPU time to analyze1,7.

objects: linear mixed model; relatedness; population structure
conclusion: The sampling-model framework is a linear mixed model used to account for relatedness and population structure.
scope: Main text identifies the model class; its explicit likelihood and distributional assumptions reside in Online Methods not present in the retrieved text.
span: There is an increasing interest in using linear mixed models (LMMs, also known as mixed linear models, or MLMs) to test for association in genome-wide association studies (GWAS), because of their demonstrated effectiveness in accounting for relatedness among samples and in controlling for population stratification and other confounding factors1–7.

objects: genotype data; tested SNPs; relatedness matrix
conclusion: GEMMA requires complete or imputed genotype data for all SNPs.
scope: Required genotype completeness; not a summary-statistic-only input contract.
span: Briefly, the method requires complete or imputed genotype data12,13 for all SNPs, and involves only one eigen-decomposition of the relatedness matrix at the beginning (computational complexity O(n3)).

objects: relatedness matrix; eigendecomposition; SNP vector; objective derivatives
assumptions: n individuals; full-rank genome-wide relatedness matrix; one tested SNP at a time
conclusion: One initial eigendecomposition is followed by quadratic-cost matrix-vector operations per SNP and linear-cost derivative evaluations in each optimization iteration.
scope: Algorithmic operation counts in n; does not state an iteration bound or global optimum theorem.
span: Briefly, the method requires complete or imputed genotype data12,13 for all SNPs, and involves only one eigen-decomposition of the relatedness matrix at the beginning (computational complexity O(n3)). For each SNP tested, it effectively replaces the expensive additional eigen-decomposition step in EMMA with one matrix and vector multiplication (computational complexity O(n2)). After this, like EMMA, each iteration of the following optimization step requires cheap operations (complexity O(n)) to evaluate both first and second derivatives of the target functions.

objects: Wald statistic; likelihood ratio statistic; sample size n
assumptions: same LMM analysis as EMMA; usual genome-wide relatedness matrix for the stated quadratic cost
conclusion: GEMMA computes numerically identical Wald or likelihood ratio statistics to EMMA with quadratic rather than cubic per-SNP cost in n.
scope: Author-stated computational exactness relative to EMMA; not a guarantee of finite-sample null calibration.
span: Here, we present a new, more efficient, method for exact calculations that provides numerically identical results to EMMA (i.e. exact Wald or likelihood ratio test statistics) but is roughly n times faster (computation time per SNP, when using the usual genome-wide relatedness matrix, is quadratic in the number of individuals, with run time similar to EMMAX).

objects: null-model LMM residuals; standard linear model
assumptions: GRAMMAR approximation to LMM association testing
conclusion: GRAMMAR estimates residuals under the null LMM and then tests those residuals as phenotypes with a standard linear model.
scope: Named earlier approximation contrasted with exact GEMMA.
span: Probably the simplest and fastest of these approximations, GRAMMAR (Genome-wide Rapid Association using Mixed Model And Regression), implemented in the software GenABEL9, first estimates the residuals from the LMM under the null model, and then treats these residuals as phenotypes for further genome-wide analysis by a standard linear model10.

objects: variance components estimated under the null
conclusion: P3D avoids repeated variance-component estimation by reusing null-model estimates for each test.
scope: Named approximation contrasted with exact GEMMA.
span: Zhang et al7 use P3D (Population Parameters Previously Determined) which avoids repeatedly estimating variance components when performing each test by simply using the pre-estimated variance components from the null model; their method is implemented in the software TASSEL.

conclusion: EMMAX avoids repeated variance-component estimation by fixing heritability at its null-model estimate.
scope: Named approximation contrasted with exact GEMMA.
span: Kang et al1 also avoid repeatedly estimating variance components by a slightly different strategy, which keeps the heritability estimated from the null model fixed when testing individual SNPs. Their approach is implemented in the software EMMAX (EMMA eXpedited).

assumptions: mixed model with more than one random effect in the paper's variance-component terminology
conclusion: The computational trick used by GEMMA does not apply to mixed models with more than one random effect, where approximations may remain necessary.
scope: Scope limitation of this computational method; no claimed extension to multiple structured random effects.
span: However, in some settings, and specifically for mixed models with more than one random effect (variance component), the computational trick used by GEMMA does not apply, and approximations along the lines of EMMAX may remain necessary.

objects: likelihood; first and second derivatives; Newton-Raphson; Brent
assumptions: comparison with the Lippert et al algorithm
conclusion: Efficient derivative evaluation enables Newton-Raphson optimization, whose theoretical convergence is described as quadratic rather than Brent's super-linear convergence.
scope: Author-stated convergence-rate comparison; convergence conditions and global-optimum guarantees are not supplied in this main-text sentence.
span: The main additional contribution of our work here beyond that in Lippert et al is that we provide, and make use of, efficient methods for evaluation of not only the likelihood, but also both its first and second derivatives. This allows us to make use of the Newton--Raphson optimization method, which has better theoretical convergence properties than Brent's algorithm (quadratic, vs super-linear), potentially reducing per-SNP computation time by reducing the number of iterations required for convergence, t.

objects: LMM likelihood; decomposition; exact statistics; computational complexity
assumptions: Lippert et al method combined with Brent optimization
conclusion: The FaST-LMM approach uses one decomposition and Brent optimization to compute exact LMM test statistics at effectively the same complexity as GEMMA.
scope: Comparison of exact methods; excludes the separate low-rank approximation.
span: While this work was in review, Lippert et al8 also published an efficient method for computing likelihoods for LMMs that, like our method, requires only one singular value decomposition of the relatedness matrix. They use this method, in combination with Brent's optimization algorithm, to produce an algorithm for computing exact test statistics with effectively the same computational complexity as GEMMA: O(mn2+cn2+pn2+ptc2n), as in Table 1.

objects: low-rank relatedness; association p values; complexity in n
assumptions: FaST-LMM variant replacing the usual relatedness matrix with a low-rank matrix
conclusion: The low-rank FaST-LMM variant can scale linearly in n but changes p values, making it not directly comparable to GEMMA or EMMA using the usual matrix.
scope: Changed covariance model; computational equivalence does not establish identical tests.
span: (Lippert et al8 also suggest a further innovation, using a low-rank relatedness matrix in place of the usual relatedness matrix computed from all SNPs genome-wide, that produces an algorithm that is linear in n, and so feasible for very large GWAS samples containing more than 100,000 individuals; however changing the relatedness matrix in this way changes the resulting p values appreciably, and in this sense this linear complexity algorithm is not directly comparable with either GEMMA or EMMA; see below for further discussion.)

objects: relatedness matrix rank; structure control; type I error; power
assumptions: HMDP and WTCCC examples using lower-rank relatedness matrices
conclusion: In the two examined datasets, lower-rank relatedness matrices appear to compromise control of sample structure, so matrix choice affects statistical as well as computational efficiency.
scope: Author-reported empirical observation in two examples, not a universal theorem about low rank.
span: However, we note that changing the relatedness matrix can produce much larger changes in p values than, for example, the differences between EMMAX and exact calculations (e.g. Supplementary Fig. 2), and for both the HMDP and WTCCC data using a lower-rank relatedness matrix seems to compromise the ability of the LMM to control for sample structure (Supplementary Table 1). Thus choice of relatedness matrix could affect statistical efficiency (both power, and correct control of type I error due to stratification or relatedness) as well as computational efficiency.

objects: relatedness matrix; rank r; sample size n
assumptions: usual matrix computed from genome-wide SNPs versus a lower-rank choice
conclusion: The usual genome-wide relatedness matrix is typically full rank, while choosing a lower-rank matrix reduces decomposition cost and sometimes memory.
scope: Relatedness-matrix choice is a modeling degree of freedom; lower rank changes the model.
span: Here we have focused on computations using the usual relatedness matrix, computed from all SNPs genome-wide, whose rank, r, is typically equal to the number of individuals n. However, as noted by Lippert et al8, if a lower-rank relatedness matrix is used then this reduces computing time (computational complexity of the singular value decomposition can scale with nr2) and in some cases memory requirements (e.g. Lippert et al.8 suggest using a relatedness matrix based on only a few thousand SNPs; this has the nice property that required singular value decompositions can be done without computing the n by n relatedness matrix itself).

objects: compressed MLM; individual clusters; lower-rank relatedness matrix
assumptions: clustering individuals as in Zhang et al reference 7
conclusion: The cited compressed MLM approach is reported to reduce computation and potentially increase power by constructing a lower-rank matrix through clustering individuals.
scope: Attributed claim about a named earlier approach; not a general guarantee for arbitrary low-rank matrices.
span: Interestingly, statistical and computational considerations may not necessarily conflict: for example,7 suggest that use of compressed MLM, which yields a lower-rank relatedness matrix by clustering individuals, can both reduce computation and increase power compared with the full-rank matrix.
